sections.content: Savannah, Georgia has quietly become one of the most attractive real estate markets in the Southeast. With its historic charm, booming tourism, and a growing port economy, the city offers something for every type of investor — from wholesalers hunting their first deal to seasoned landlords building long-term wealth. Whether you're local or looking from out of state, finding real estate deals in Savannah GA is more achievable than you might think. If you're newer to the game, start with our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide to get your foundation solid before diving into a specific market.
Savannah GA Market Overview: Why Investors Are Paying Attention

Savannah sits at the intersection of several powerful economic forces. The Port of Savannah is one of the largest and fastest-growing container ports in the United States, driving thousands of logistics, manufacturing, and service jobs into the metro area. Meanwhile, Savannah College of Art and Design (SCAD) brings in roughly 15,000 students annually, and tourism — centered on the city's famous squares, riverfront, and historic district — generates over $3 billion in economic activity each year. All of this creates consistent housing demand, which is exactly what real estate investors need.

As of late 2024, the median home price in Savannah sits around $310,000, up from roughly $240,000 just three years ago. That's a 29% increase, yet prices remain significantly below coastal markets like Charleston, SC ($430,000+) or Jacksonville, FL ($360,000+). For investors doing the math, Savannah still offers real runway for appreciation while delivering solid cash flow numbers today. Explore active deal flow and current listings on our [Savannah GA market page](aiwholesail.com/markets/savannah-ga).
Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Deals in Savannah GA

Not all of Savannah's zip codes are created equal. Knowing where to focus your search can mean the difference between a home run deal and a money pit. Here are the neighborhoods that savvy investors are watching right now.
Starland District and Thomas Square

These two adjacent neighborhoods have undergone rapid gentrification over the past five years. Historic bungalows and craftsman-style homes that sold for $120,000 in 2018 are now fetching $280,000–$350,000. There's still a pipeline of distressed properties here, making it a strong target for fix-and-flip investors who can move quickly.
Eastside and Carver Village

Located east of downtown, these areas offer lower entry prices in the $150,000–$220,000 range with strong rental demand from blue-collar workers tied to the port and local manufacturing. Cash-on-cash returns of 8–12% are achievable for buy-and-hold investors who buy right. Distressed properties here are plentiful, which makes it a prime hunting ground for wholesalers.
Ardsley Park and Midtown Savannah

These are Savannah's more established, middle-class neighborhoods with strong owner-occupant demand. Properties here make excellent long-term rentals, and values have been steadily climbing. If you're targeting the BRRRR strategy — Buy, Rehab, Rent, Refinance, Repeat — this area can work well with the right deal structure.
Pooler and Richmond Hill (Suburbs)

The Savannah metro extends well into the suburbs, and areas like Pooler and Richmond Hill are absorbing enormous population growth. New construction is heavy here, but investors who can find older, dated homes on larger lots can often negotiate below-market deals from long-time owners looking to sell without the hassle of listing.
Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Savannah
Wholesale Deals

Savannah has a healthy wholesale market, particularly in Eastside, Carver Village, and older suburban pockets. Motivated sellers — often facing probate situations, tax liens, or deferred maintenance — are open to cash offers below market value. A typical wholesale deal in Savannah might involve buying at $130,000 and assigning the contract for a $10,000–$20,000 fee to a cash buyer who plans to rehab the home. If you're new to this strategy, read our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide before you start making offers. Finding these deals requires consistent outreach — direct mail, driving for dollars, and increasingly, data-driven platforms that surface motivated sellers before they hit the MLS. Learning [how to find off-market real estate deals](aiwholesail.com/guides/off-market-real-estate-deals) is the single biggest edge you can develop in a competitive market like Savannah.
Fix and Flip

Savannah's older housing stock — many homes date back to the 1920s through 1970s — creates a steady supply of flip candidates. The key is buying at the right price. A common flip formula in this market: target homes with an ARV (after-repair value) of $300,000–$380,000, buy at 65–70% of ARV minus repairs, and budget $40,000–$80,000 for rehab depending on condition. Use our free [ARV Calculator](aiwholesail.com/tools/arv-calculator) to quickly estimate what a property will be worth after repairs, so you never overpay on the front end.
Rental Properties and Short-Term Rentals

Savannah's tourist economy makes short-term rentals (Airbnb, VRBO) extremely lucrative — especially in and around the Historic District. A well-positioned vacation rental can generate $3,500–$6,000 per month in gross revenue. However, the city does regulate STRs, so always verify licensing requirements before purchasing. For traditional long-term rentals, expect to collect $1,200–$1,800 per month for a 3-bedroom home in most investor-friendly neighborhoods, with vacancy rates staying low due to consistent demand from students, port workers, and military families at nearby Fort Stewart.

Before making any offer in Savannah, always run the numbers through a deal calculator. Our free [Wholesale Deal Calculator](aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) lets you plug in purchase price, repair costs, ARV, and holding costs to instantly see if a deal pencils out. Never trust your gut alone — the math has to work.
Savannah Real Estate Market Trends to Watch in 2024–2025

items: Population growth is accelerating: Chatham County added over 8,000 new residents between 2022 and 2024, driven by remote workers and port-related job growth.
Inventory remains tight: Active listings in Savannah are still roughly 30% below pre-pandemic levels, keeping upward pressure on prices.
Interest rate sensitivity: Higher mortgage rates have slowed owner-occupant buying, but cash investors have stepped in — meaning competition for distressed deals is real.
Suburban expansion: Pooler is one of the fastest-growing cities in Georgia, and infrastructure investment is following, supporting long-term property values.
Short-term rental demand is holding strong: Post-pandemic travel has not slowed in Savannah — occupancy rates for STRs remain above 70% year-round in prime areas.

Institutional investors are circling: Single-family rental funds have begun buying in the metro, which typically signals a market is maturing — a good sign for appreciation, but a warning to move sooner rather than later.

Practical Tips for Out-of-State Investors Targeting Savannah
Savannah is one of the more investor-friendly cities in the South, but out-of-state buyers do face unique challenges. Here's how to stack the odds in your favor before you wire a single dollar.

items: Build your local team first: You need a boots-on-the-ground property manager, a reliable general contractor, and a real estate attorney familiar with Georgia contracts. Don't skip this step.
Understand Georgia's landlord-tenant laws: Georgia is generally landlord-friendly, but eviction timelines and security deposit rules differ from other states. Know the rules before you buy.

Visit before you buy: Savannah's neighborhoods can change dramatically block by block. A property that looks great on Zillow may sit across from a problem block. Drive the streets or hire a local scout.
Focus on off-market deals: The best deals in Savannah rarely hit the MLS. Build relationships with local wholesalers, probate attorneys, and estate sale companies to get first access.

Factor in flood insurance: Parts of Savannah sit in FEMA flood zones. Always check FEMA maps before purchasing, and budget flood insurance into your carrying costs — it can run $1,500–$4,000+ annually.
Use data to your advantage: Platforms like AIWholesail can surface motivated seller leads and deal data across Savannah zip codes, saving you months of manual research.

sections.content: Once you've identified potential deals, the next critical step is running a thorough analysis. Learn [how to analyze real estate deals like a pro](aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals) so you can quickly separate the winners from the time-wasters — especially important when you're evaluating deals remotely.

When investing out of state, always hire a local property manager before closing — not after. A good PM will flag red flags in a property inspection that an out-of-town buyer might miss, and they'll already have a tenant pipeline ready to go the day you close.
Is Savannah GA Right for Your Investment Strategy?

Savannah checks a lot of boxes: diversified economy, tourism-driven rental demand, below-coastal-market pricing, and a steady stream of distressed inventory for wholesalers and flippers. It's not a zero-competition market — nothing worth having is — but for investors who do their homework, build local relationships, and use smart tools to find deals faster, Savannah still offers real opportunity in 2024 and beyond. The window won't stay open forever. Institutional money is watching. Individual investors who move with both speed and discipline are the ones who will win.
